annotations.keyFindings: In 240 paired emergency department histories, technicians recorded 91 percent and pharmacists 93 percent of medications correctly.
Technician-led discharge reconciliation found discrepancies in 34 percent of 1,120 discharges; pharmacists confirmed 88 percent; pharmacist reconciliation time fell by about 60 percent.
annotations.limitations: No patient outcomes; three wards of one hospital.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 46 programme descriptions, training ranged from four hours to 12 weeks, 29 required a competency assessment and 11 described maintaining competence.
annotations.limitations: Descriptions, not evaluations; publication bias likely.

annotations.keyFindings: Only 5 of 14 jurisdictions allowed technicians to document discharge discrepancies without a pharmacist present; none allowed them to resolve discrepancies with prescribers.
annotations.limitations: Regulations changed during the study in 4 jurisdictions.

annotations.keyFindings: Rural hospitals using technicians reported histories for 78 percent of admissions against 41 percent without; 12 reported technician discharge reconciliation.
Readmission fell from 14.2 to 13.1 percent after technician-supported discharge reconciliation, within secular variation; pharmacists agreed with 95 percent of sampled reconciliations.
annotations.limitations: Before-after with a concurrent template change.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 150 evaluations, discrepancies were the most common outcome and definitions varied; patient-reported outcomes appeared in 4 percent.
annotations.limitations: Catalogue of outcomes, not of effects.

claims.text: In emergency department medication histories, technicians recorded 91 percent of medications correctly and pharmacists 93 percent.
claims.passage: technicians recorded 91 percent of medications correctly and pharmacists 93 percent
claims.interpretation: Supports charting accuracy by transition; says nothing about discharge.

claims.text: Technician-led discharge reconciliation identified unintentional discrepancies in 34 percent of discharges, and pharmacists confirmed 88 percent of those referred.
claims.passage: Technicians identified at least one unintentional discrepancy in 34 percent of discharges; pharmacists confirmed 88 percent of the discrepancies referred.
claims.interpretation: The discharge role exists elsewhere and should be charted with its supervision model.

claims.text: Only 5 of 14 jurisdictions allowed technicians to compare lists and document discrepancies at discharge without a pharmacist present.
claims.passage: only 5 allowed technicians to compare lists and document discrepancies at discharge without a pharmacist present
claims.interpretation: Regulatory scope must be charted by jurisdiction and date.

claims.text: Definitions of a medication discrepancy varied between evaluations of medication reconciliation.
claims.passage: Definitions of a discrepancy varied between evaluations
claims.interpretation: Chart each report's definition rather than comparing counts.

synthesis: Seven records from the second recorded search, appraised at abstract level; the first search returned none. Technicians take admission histories with accuracy close to pharmacists', and one hospital reports technician-led discharge reconciliation that found discrepancies in a third of discharges and freed pharmacist time. Training and supervision models vary widely, regulators differ on whether technicians may document discharge discrepancies, and outcome definitions are inconsistent. Patient outcomes are rarely measured. The field is scattered, which suits a scoping review that charts tasks, supervision, measures and scope.
gradeRationale: Descriptive and before-after studies, programme descriptions and regulatory comparisons; low certainty for accuracy, very low for patient outcomes.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims with passages; certainty low; Scan now complete on retrieved records.
